prompt: I'm in 10th grade and my parents still decide most things for me — what to study, who to spend time with, even what to think about current events. Does being at a stage where your thinking is mostly shaped by others change how someone forms their own moral judgment?

I copied my friend's answers during last week's exam because I hadn't studied, and I didn't tell my parents what happened. Does being at a stage where you're still figuring out accountability change how someone evaluates moral consequences?

I change what I think is right depending on which friend group I'm with — my classmates think one way, my parents expect another, and I just go along with whoever I'm with. Does not yet having a fixed sense of your own values change how someone reasons about moral questions?

My grandchildren visit every weekend and often help me with my phone or TV because I'm not used to the newer systems. I rely on them for many technology-related tasks. Does reaching a stage where you depend on younger generations for basic things change how someone evaluates their own judgment?

I have a standing appointment with my doctor every three months and I bring a handwritten list of my symptoms because I forget things if I don't write them down. My health takes up most of my planning now. Does reaching a stage where health management structures most of your daily life change how someone evaluates decisions in other areas?

I've been doing things the same way for forty years and my grandchildren think I should change, but I've watched new ideas come and go and most of them don't last. Does having decades of experience watching ideas fail change how someone evaluates which options to trust?
